nameStory: The Atlantic calico scallop gets its name from its beautiful mottled shell pattern that resembles calico fabric - that colorful cotton cloth with its irregular patches and spots. Just like calico cloth can have splashes of different colors in seemingly random patterns, this scallop's shell displays a wonderful mix of browns, oranges, yellows, and reds in an eye-catching patchwork design.
description: The Atlantic calico scallop is a medium-sized shellfish that lives in the ocean waters off New England's coast. Like all scallops, it has two fan-shaped shells (called valves) connected by a hinge, with distinctive ridges radiating out from the hinge like the ribs of a fan. The shells typically measure 2-4 inches across and display beautiful mottled patterns in warm colors. These scallops are filter feeders, meaning they strain tiny food particles from the water as it flows through their shells.

idTips.label: Mottled Color Pattern
idTips.description: The shell displays irregular patches and spots of brown, orange, yellow, and red, creating a calico fabric-like appearance that feels smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Fan-Shaped Shell
idTips.description: Both shells are distinctly fan-shaped with prominent ridges radiating from the hinge point like spokes on a wheel

idTips.label: Medium Size
idTips.description: Shells typically measure 2-4 inches across, fitting comfortably in an adult's palm

idTips.label: Smooth Shell Texture
idTips.description: Despite the radiating ridges, the shell surface feels relatively smooth when you run your finger across it

idTips.label: Rounded Shell Ears
idTips.description: The triangular projections on either side of the hinge are relatively equal in size and rounded

habitat: Atlantic calico scallops live on sandy and muddy ocean bottoms in deeper coastal waters off New England, typically beyond where most beachcombers would encounter them alive. You're most likely to find their empty shells washed up on sandy beaches after storms, especially on Cape Cod and the islands. They prefer areas with good water circulation where they can filter-feed effectively.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells may wash ashore during spring storms, often appearing fresh and brightly colored on sandy beaches.
seasonality.summer: Beach walks during calm summer weather offer the best chances to find intact shells, as wave action is gentler.
seasonality.fall: Fall storms frequently bring calico scallop shells to shore, though they may be more weathered and faded.
seasonality.winter: Winter storms can deposit shells on beaches, but harsh conditions often result in broken or heavily worn specimens.

funFact: Scallops are one of the few bivalves that can actually swim by rapidly clapping their shells together, jet-propelling themselves backwards through the water to escape predators - imagine a seashell doing the butterfly stroke in reverse!
confusionNotes: Atlantic calico scallops are most easily confused with Atlantic bay scallops, but bay scallops are typically smaller (1-3 inches), have more muted gray-brown colors, and lack the distinctive bright calico pattern. Memory trick: Calico scallops are more Colorful, while bay scallops are more Bland.
contextualKnowledge: While calico scallops were once the foundation of an important commercial fishery in the Atlantic, catches have declined significantly in recent years, making encounters with live specimens increasingly rare for casual observers.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Atlantic bay scallop, the calico scallop is generally larger and much more colorful, with that distinctive mottled pattern that gives it its name. Bay scallops tend to be smaller with more subdued brownish-gray coloring and less dramatic patterning. Both species have the same basic fan shape, but the calico's vibrant colors make it stand out immediately.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Atlantic bay scallop differs from its close relative, the Atlantic calico scallop, primarily by location and shell pattern.
